title: Hydrogels in Pharmacy and Medicine: An Illustrated Review of Preparation Methods, Process Control and Drug Delivery Applications
content: Hydrogels, three-dimensional hydrophilic polymer networks that can imbibe large volumes of water or biological fluids without dissolving, have become one of the most versatile platforms in pharmaceutical and biomaterial science. Their high water content, soft tissue-like mechanics, biocompatibility and tunable network architecture allow them to be engineered as topical, ophthalmic, mucosal, oral and injectable dosage forms and as scaffolds for regenerative medicine. This illustrated review provides a critical, practice-oriented account of the field, with particular emphasis on how hydrogel dosage forms are prepared. Physical cross-linking methods (ionic gelation, polyelectrolyte complexation, thermoresponsive gelation, freeze–thaw cycling and supramolecular assembly) and chemical cross-linking methods (free-radical and photo-initiated polymerization, small-molecule cross-linkers, click and dynamic covalent chemistries, and enzyme-mediated and radiation cross-linking) are examined in terms of their mechanisms, typical materials and conditions, critical process parameters, advantages and limitations. The preparation of conventional pharmaceutical gels based on carbomers, cellulose ethers, poloxamers and polysaccharides is described step by step, together with drug-loading strategies, processing into beads, micro- and nanogels, films, sponges, microneedles and printed constructs, and a troubleshooting guide for the most frequent formulation failures. Advanced architectures that overcome the intrinsic weakness of conventional networks, including hybrid, interpenetrating, nanocomposite, double-network and Tetra-PEG hydrogels, are then discussed, followed by the characterization and quality-control methods needed to establish critical quality attributes such as gel fraction, swelling and mesh size, rheology, morphology, release kinetics, stability, microbiological quality and biocompatibility. The review subsequently analyzes drug release mechanisms, route-specific delivery strategies, stimuli-responsive and hierarchical systems, the selection of drug candidates with reference to physicochemical properties and the Biopharmaceutics Classification System, and applications in tissue engineering and wound care. Finally, clinically approved products and the main translational barriers, namely mechanical fragility, burst release, residual reagents, sterilization, batch-to-batch variability and regulatory classification, are critically evaluated to identify realistic routes towards next-generation, clinically useful hydrogel dosage forms.
